newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand plans decrees to beat economy woes-paper.
newsitem.headline: Thailand plans decrees to beat economy woes-paper.

text.p: Thailand plans to issue executive decrees to facilitate mergers of cash-strapped finance firms and to set up permanant measures to protect the baht from speculative attacks, a local newspaper reported on Monday.

The Bangkok Post quoted a deputy finance minister as saying that the decrees would also detail steps to bail out the depressed property sector through a secondary mortgage scheme and by securitisation.
A government spokesman confirmed the decrees were planned but told Reuters he had no details.

The newspaper quoted deputy finance minister Thawatvong Na ChiangMai as saying that the plan to issue the decrees were reached at a meeting late on Sunday between Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya and other senior officials.
"Mr. Thawatvong said at least five decrees would be announced by the prime minister when he gets approval from the cabinet tomorrow," the newspaper said.
It added that officials agreed at Sunday night's meeting to seek endorsement for the decrees from the Thai cabinet to "prevent any possible negative political repercussions".
Thailand's prime minister has authority under current laws to invoke special legislative measures when there are urgent economic or security needs, the Bangkok Post said.
Last week, Thanong Bidaya was appointed Finance Minister to replace the respected Amnuay Viravan who quit after differences with political rivals in the ruling six-party coalition.
The country is going through its worst economic crisis in over a decade, with the embattled baht under speculative attack because of foreign perceptions it should be devalued.
After the last attack in mid-May, the central bank imposed currency controls to cut off baht supply to foreign speculators from local sources.
The Thai stock market is at eight year lows and exports have slowed sharply.
Private economists have put economic growth at between three and five percent for 1997, versus 6.4 percent in 1996.
